opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the questions I think about most, because it's a real concern. When you run a simulation with many agents interacting over many time steps, any small error in one agent's behavior doesn't stay local. It gets passed to other agents, they react to it, and over time it can push the whole system somewhere unrealistic. A slightly off-character response early on can snowball into a town that looks nothing like a real community.

A few things shape how I think about it.

First, it depends on what you want from the simulation. If you're trying to predict an exact trajectory, like exactly what person A says to person B on day three, compounding errors will hurt you badly, and you probably shouldn't trust that level of detail. But that usually isn't the useful question. What we care about is the aggregate: the distribution of outcomes, the patterns of behavior, how a population responds to an intervention. At that level, many individual errors wash out or partly cancel, much as they do in traditional agent-based modeling or in social science more broadly.

Second, convergence is informative. When simulations started from somewhat different conditions, or run with different random seeds, keep arriving at similar outcomes, that tells you the dynamics are driven by something structural rather than by noise in any single agent's behavior. That gives me more confidence. When runs diverge wildly, that's a signal too. It tells you either the system is chaotic, which may be true of the real-world phenomenon, or that your agents aren't grounded enough.

Third, grounding the agents is probably the biggest lever. In our more recent work, we built agents from in-depth interviews with real people and then checked how well those agents reproduced the people's own responses on surveys and experiments. The closer each agent is anchored to a real individual, the less room there is for drift. Errors still happen, but they're bounded by an actual human reference point rather than floating freely on whatever the model's default persona is.

Finally, I think we have to be honest about validation. You can't simply assume a converged simulation reflects reality. You have to check it against real data wherever you can, ideally on cases where you know the ground truth, before you trust it on cases where you don't. That's how other simulation fields matured, whether weather forecasting or epidemiology, and I think generative agent simulations need to go through the same discipline.

r001.rationale: The response says the impact of errors depends on whether the goal is an exact trajectory or aggregate patterns, but does not state that whether a simulation converges or diverges depends on the research question.

r002.rationale: It says similar outcomes across runs suggest structural dynamics and that grounding can reduce drift, but does not explain that attraction toward a convergent outcome can outweigh compounding errors in a sufficiently faithful simulation.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention simulated human networks developing hubs.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Yeah, that's something I think about a lot, because it's really the central tension of this whole line of work. When you build a generative agent, you're asking a model to make a decision, then another decision conditioned on that one, and so on, potentially thousands of times. And every one of those steps has some probability of being slightly off. So the naive worry is that these errors just stack up, and by the end of the simulation you're nowhere near anything that resembles human behavior.

What I've come to believe, though, is that it depends a lot on whether the thing you're simulating has a kind of attractor to it. Human behavior is actually remarkably forgiving in that sense. If an agent wakes up fifteen minutes late because the model misjudged something, that doesn't send the day spiraling into chaos. The agent still gets coffee, still goes to work, still runs into their neighbor. There's a structure to daily life, and to social life, that pulls behavior back toward something sensible. So in a lot of our simulations, errors don't compound so much as they get absorbed. The system converges because the underlying human process it's modeling also converges. People are robust.

The place where I get much more worried is when you're using these simulations to make claims about aggregate outcomes, especially in the social science setting. There, you're not just asking "does this look plausible," you're asking "does the distribution of behaviors match the distribution of real behaviors." And if the model has a systematic bias, say it's a little more agreeable than real people, or a little more consistent in its political views than real people are, that's not random noise that washes out. That's a directional error, and it compounds in the sense that every agent carries it, and the aggregate reflects it. Convergence can actually be misleading there, because the simulation looks stable, it looks like it settled into something, but it settled into the wrong thing.

So the way I think about it is that convergence is not evidence of correctness. What you really want is to validate at multiple levels. Does the individual agent's behavior match the individual it's based on? Does the population-level behavior match what you'd observe in the real population? And importantly, does it replicate known results, things we already have ground truth for from the social sciences? If you can get agreement at all those levels, then I start to trust the convergence. If you only have the top level, I'd be pretty cautious about what you conclude from it.

r001.rationale: The response says convergence depends on whether the simulated process has an attractor and distinguishes plausibility from aggregate accuracy. It does not state that convergence or divergence depends on the research question being asked.

r002.rationale: The response explains that human behavior has structure that pulls agents back toward sensible outcomes, so errors can be absorbed and the simulation can converge. This communicates that attraction toward a convergent outcome can outweigh compounding errors.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss human networks reliably developing hubs.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: converge to what? A simulation can settle into a stable pattern and still be wrong. So convergence alone doesn’t tell us that errors have washed out. An early mistake might push the simulation toward a different outcome, and subsequent interactions can reinforce it.

But errors don’t necessarily compound in every case, either. Some get corrected through interaction, or don’t matter much for the particular outcome you’re studying. I’d want to distinguish whether we’re trying to predict an individual’s exact trajectory or capture a broader pattern across a population. Those require different kinds of accuracy.

The way I’d approach it is to perturb the simulation: change the initial conditions, introduce small errors, run it multiple times, and see whether the conclusions hold. And then compare those conclusions with observations outside the simulation. If a result is robust across runs but consistently disagrees with reality, that’s a stable modeling error, not evidence that the simulation works.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes individual trajectories from broader population patterns, but does not say that whether a simulation converges or diverges depends on the research question.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible error correction and robustness, but does not explain that attraction toward a convergent outcome can outweigh compounding errors in a sufficiently faithful simulation.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about human networks reliably developing hubs when human behavior is reproduced accurately.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is what the simulation is converging to. Convergence by itself doesn’t mean that you’ve arrived at something that accurately reflects human behavior. You can have a simulation that settles into a very stable pattern because of a bias in the model, and that bias can get reinforced as agents interact with one another.

So I would separate two questions: Is the simulation stable, and is it valid for the question we’re trying to answer? An error might wash out over time, or it might change an early interaction that sends the whole simulation down a different path. You want to test that by perturbing the initial conditions, running multiple simulations, and checking against observations from people where you can.

The goal isn’t necessarily to reproduce every individual action. It’s to understand which conclusions remain reliable despite those errors, and where the simulation stops giving us evidence we should trust.

r001.rationale: The response says stability and validity are separate and validity depends on the research question, but it does not state that convergence versus divergence depends on that question.

r002.rationale: It says errors may wash out or redirect the simulation, but does not explain that attraction toward a convergent outcome can outweigh compounding errors in a sufficiently faithful simulation.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about simulated human networks developing hubs.
